claims.claim: Adopt a 'low floor, high ceiling' design: start every lesson with a basic activity all students can complete to secure core goals, then offer optional extension challenges so early finishers stay stretched.

Share pre-written starter code via micro:bit Classroom so struggling learners are not faced with a blank screen; teachers can set up the first few blocks and share them with less-able pupils to help them get started.

Use mixed-ability pairs or small groups (1 device to 2-3 learners) where more-able pupils help peers, and use pair programming (driver/navigator) so no one is left behind while experts still build skills.

For conceptual struggles, ask the pupil to explain what the code should do and walk through it line by line to find bugs; if they cannot, model metacognitive troubleshooting aloud, then note the concept to reinforce later.

Use tiered 'Mild / Medium / Spicy' learning objectives within a single lesson so struggling learners meet the Mild goal (recall/use the block) while advanced learners reach Spicy (create/modify their own program).
Give groups red/yellow/green cup progress indicators so the teacher can prioritise pupils who are completely stuck, while slightly-confused pupils keep debugging and know when help is coming.

For learners who find shake or button presses hard, swap the input event block for alternatives such as the touch-sensitive logo, sound activation, or an external switch, adapting any if/then or shake project to individual capability.

Stretch advanced learners by letting them create their own challenge from the same block set (e.g. combine random with shake to build a game, or design original LED art) rather than stopping at the modelled task.
